summary: The survivors learn they are on Malta, where local people show extraordinary kindness. A viper fastens to Paul's hand; observers first call him a murderer pursued by Justice and then a god when he remains unharmed. Paul heals Publius's father and other sick islanders, and the company receives supplies. After winter they sail to Italy, where Roman believers meet Paul and give him courage. Under guarded house arrest Paul summons local Jewish leaders, insists he has done nothing against his people or ancestral customs, and says he wears a chain for Israel's hope. A day-long scriptural discussion produces mixed responses. Paul cites Isaiah's calloused-hearing passage, announces that Gentiles will listen, and spends two years welcoming everyone, proclaiming God's kingdom and teaching Jesus with all boldness, ‘unhindered.’
whyItMatters: Acts reaches Rome without declaring Rome the end of the earth or resolving Paul's trial. The final scene keeps Israel's hope, Jewish disagreement, Gentile hearing, imperial chains, open hospitality, kingdom proclamation, and Jesus teaching in one room. The last word, akōlytōs—unhindered—does not pretend Paul is free; it declares that custody cannot close the mission and turns the unfinished horizon toward the reader.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator completing the Jerusalem-to-Rome movement while leaving Paul's legal outcome unstated
context.audience: Readers asked to continue discerning and embodying unhindered witness beyond the narrative
context.date: The story reaches Paul's two-year Roman house arrest, commonly placed in the early 60s
context.setting: Malta, Syracuse, Rhegium, Puteoli, the Appian Way, and rented quarters in Rome
context.literaryForm: Island rescue and healing narrative, final travel itinerary, house-arrest dialogue, scriptural speech, and open-ended summary

outline.heading: Malta's people welcome the survivors; Paul survives the viper and heals
The voyage reaches Italy and believers encourage Paul on the Appian Way
Paul explains his chain and Israel's hope to Roman Jewish leaders
A day-long scriptural witness ends in mixed response and unhindered teaching

keyVerses.text: For this cause therefore I asked to see you and to speak with you. For because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.”
keyVerses.why: Paul interprets his imprisonment through continuity with Israel's hope, not rejection of his people.

keyVerses.text: “Be it known therefore to you that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen.”
keyVerses.why: Gentile hearing continues Acts' outward movement without making every Gentile receptive or Israel discarded.

keyVerses.text: preaching God’s Kingdom and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.
keyVerses.why: The final adverb makes constrained yet open witness the book's enduring horizon.

questions.question: Why does the WEB call Malta's residents ‘natives,’ while older translations say ‘barbarians’?
questions.answer: The Greek barbaroi means people whose speech was not Greek, not necessarily savage or uncivilized. Luke immediately praises their philanthrōpia—extraordinary human kindness—as they welcome wet, cold strangers. ‘Natives’ avoids English barbarian's insult but can hide the ancient language distinction.

questions.question: What does the islanders' reaction to the viper reveal?
questions.answer: They interpret the bite through personified Dikē, Justice: although Paul escaped the sea, moral retribution must catch a murderer. When he remains unharmed, they swing to calling him a god. Luke exposes snap theology based on changing circumstances; Paul neither confesses murder nor accepts divinity.

questions.question: Was there really a venomous viper on Malta?
questions.answer: Modern Malta lacks native venomous snakes, prompting proposals about species extinction, ancient naming, cargo transport, a nonvenomous snake mistaken by observers, or another island identification. The narrative's point is the expected lethal bite and Paul's survival, not zoological classification. The historical question is legitimate but the text cannot settle present ecology.

questions.question: Does Paul heal Publius's father by prayer or laying on hands?
questions.answer: Both: Paul enters, prays, lays hands on him, and heals him. Other sick islanders then come and are cured; Luke uses different healing verbs without explaining a hierarchy. The islanders honor the travelers and supply what the voyage needs, creating reciprocal care rather than a one-directional miracle performance.

questions.question: Why mention the ship's Twin Brothers figurehead?
questions.answer: The Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, were divine patrons of sailors in Greco-Roman religion. Luke identifies the Alexandrian ship by its figurehead without saying Paul worships it. The detail gives local color and quiet irony: safe arrival is narrated under God's promise even aboard a vessel carrying pagan protective imagery.

questions.question: Why do Roman believers meeting Paul matter?
questions.answer: Brothers and sisters travel as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet the chained apostle. Seeing them, Paul thanks God and takes courage. He arrives not as an isolated heroic founder but is received by a community that already exists, likely related to the believers addressed in Romans years earlier.

questions.question: How does Paul frame his case to Rome's Jewish leaders?
questions.answer: He acts promptly, calls them brothers, says he did nothing against ‘the people’ or ancestral customs, explains that Romans found no capital case, and denies accusing his nation. His chain is ‘for the hope of Israel.’ The leaders respond that they have received no hostile report and want to hear about the disputed movement.

questions.question: Does Isaiah's hearing judgment mean God has rejected Jewish people?
questions.answer: Paul speaks after some Roman Jews are persuaded and others disbelieve, quoting Isaiah's commission within an intra-Jewish argument also used by Jesus and John. The passage diagnoses resistant hearing; it does not erase the Jewish believers present throughout Acts or Paul's own hope for Israel. Gentiles ‘will hear’ names mission confidence, not ethnic superiority or universal Gentile obedience.

questions.question: Why is verse 29 present here but absent from many modern editions?
questions.answer: Later witnesses add that after Paul's words the Jewish leaders departed with much dispute among themselves. Earlier major Greek manuscripts move directly from verse 28 to Paul's two-year ministry, and critical editions omit verse 29 from the main text. The added line makes the departure explicit but does not create the already stated disagreement.

questions.question: Why does Acts end without Paul's verdict or death?
questions.answer: Luke ends after two years of welcomed visitors, kingdom proclamation, Jesus teaching, boldness, and akōlytōs—‘without hindrance,’ the book's final word. Paul remains under guard, so ‘unhindered’ describes the word's freedom within constraint. Whether the author wrote before a verdict, chose a literary endpoint, or expected readers to know later events is debated; the ending completes Acts 1:8 while leaving witness open.

glossary.def: Greek label for non-Greek speakers; it need not imply savagery, and Luke praises their kindness.
Castor and Pollux, twin divine patrons of sailors whose image marked the Alexandrian ship.
Unhindered or without hindrance—the emphatic final word of Acts.
